summary: Before crossing the Kidron, Jesus lifts His eyes to heaven and prays for His own glory, for the eleven He is leaving, and for all who will believe through them.
key_insight: Within hours these men would run away, and Peter would deny Him. Yet Jesus tells the Father, “they have kept Your word.” He describes them by what the Father has given and done, and He asks the Father to keep them, not that they keep themselves.
story: When Jesus had finished speaking to His disciples, He lifted up His eyes to heaven and prayed aloud. “Father, the hour has come. Glorify Your Son, that Your Son also may glorify You.”

The Father had given Him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all the Father had given Him. “And this is eternal life,” He said, “that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.” He told the Father, “I have finished the work which You have given Me to do.” He asked to be glorified with the glory He had with the Father before the world was.

Then He prayed for the men around Him. He had made the Father’s name known to them. They had been the Father’s, the Father had given them to Him, and they had received His words and believed that the Father sent Him. “I pray for them,” He said. “I do not pray for the world but for those whom You have given Me, for they are Yours.”

He was leaving, and they were staying. “Holy Father, keep through Your name those whom You have given Me, that they may be one as We are.” While He was with them He had kept them, and none was lost except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled. He spoke these things so that they might have His joy fulfilled in themselves.

The world hated them because they were not of the world, just as He was not. Yet He did not ask for their escape: “I do not pray that You should take them out of the world, but that You should keep them from the evil one.” He asked, “Sanctify them by Your truth. Your word is truth.” As the Father had sent Him into the world, so He was sending them, and for their sakes He set Himself apart.

Then His prayer reached further. “I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in Me through their word.” He prayed that all of them would be one, as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, “that the world may believe that You sent Me.” He had given them the glory the Father gave Him, so that the world would know the Father had loved them as He loved the Son.

Last of all He said, “Father, I desire that they also whom You gave Me may be with Me where I am, that they may behold My glory.” The world had not known the Father, but the Son had, and these men knew that He was sent. He had made the Father’s name known and would keep doing so, “that the love with which You loved Me may be in them, and I in them.”

scene.label: Where He prayed
scene.text: In the upper room Jesus had said, “Arise, let us go from here” (John 14:31). After the prayer, John says, He went out over the Brook Kidron (John 18:1). So He prayed somewhere between: perhaps still in the room, perhaps on the way through the city. John does not say.

scene.label: Eyes lifted up
scene.text: Jews often prayed standing, with eyes raised toward heaven. Jesus did the same at the tomb of Lazarus, when He thanked the Father aloud for the sake of those listening (John 11:41–42). Here too the disciples were meant to hear.

scene.label: “The hour”
scene.text: Early in John’s Gospel, Jesus says, “My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4), and twice His enemies cannot seize Him because His hour had not yet come (7:30; 8:20). Once Greeks came seeking Him, He said, “The hour has come that the Son of Man should be glorified” (12:23). In John the hour is the cross, the resurrection and His return to the Father.

scene.label: “The son of perdition”
scene.text: The phrase means one who belongs to destruction. It refers to Judas, who had already left the supper. The Scripture Jesus had in mind is probably Psalm 41:9, which He quoted of Judas earlier that night (John 13:18). Paul uses the same title for the man of sin (2 Thessalonians 2:3).

scene.label: A priest’s prayer
scene.text: Since the 1500s this has often been called the High Priestly Prayer. Israel’s high priest carried the names of the tribes on his shoulders and over his heart when he went before God (Exodus 28:9–12, 29). “I sanctify Myself” uses the language of setting something apart for God, as a priest or a sacrifice was set apart.

witnesses.john: Only John records this prayer, the longest prayer of Jesus in the Gospels. It closes the farewell teaching of chapters 13–16 and gathers the great themes of his Gospel: the hour, glory, the world, truth, and eternal life as knowing God. John wrote “that you may believe” (John 20:31), and here Jesus prays for exactly those people, “those who will believe in Me through their word.”

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks to the Father as the Son who shared His glory before the world was made, and as the Priest who carries His people to God by name before He offers Himself for them.
seeing.living: Jesus did not ask that you be taken out of the world, but that you be kept in it, set apart by the truth, and one with every other believer. Every Christian you find hard to love is someone Jesus prayed for on the night before He died. Treat them that way.
seeing.ponder: Jesus asked the Father that you would be with Him where He is and see His glory. Is that what you most want too?

preaching.big_idea: The Son who finished His work asks the Father to keep His people until they see His glory.
outline: The Son asks to be glorified (1–5)
The Son asks the Father to keep His disciples (6–19)
The Son prays for all who will believe (20–23)
The Son asks for His people to be with Him (24–26)
preaching.watch_for: Two words carry the prayer: “world” appears nineteen times, and the Father “gave” or has “given” people to the Son again and again (vv. 2, 6, 9, 11, 12, 24). Believers live in a hostile world, but they belong to the Father, who gave them to the Son.
related_other: Hebrews 7:24–25 · He always lives to make intercession
